posts.transcript: I'd like to introduce you to the idea of cursor for film makers. That's AI agents that do a variety of analysis and tasks that perform a great deal of the. Tedious grunt work required to produce a shot list for a film, leaving the all important 20% for the human element of taste to really take over. The idea here is to make filmmaking much more efficient, cost effective and dare I say, even more fun, both for novice and professional film makers alike. Let me give you a quick tour. So starting off. We can see that the AI agents perform analysis of each scene. Building up analysis of the dramatic beats. The overall emotional arc, emotional peaks, trajectory, tempo, and so on. Now, it's also important to note that the system analyzes the characters and locations and builds profiles for each. This also builds reference material. So for example, here we can see Ronald. We know this is a background character with a little bit of dialogue. We have their voice assignment which we can change. Here's Paul, the protagonist. We have reference images for him that get used throughout this process for consistency. We have their dialogue count, their scene appearances as the main character. We can change their voice if necessary. Same thing with locations. It generates these images of the locations based on what's in the screenplay. Now once the AI has analyzed the scenes, the characters, and the locations and built reference images for consistency, it then. Deploys multiple AI agents to produce the shot list. These AI agents have essentially a film School 101 background in their context, along with all the context of the scene and the characters and locations and so on. And it produces these shots. Now we can watch the complete scene here, or we can go into our individual shots which have our anchor image. We've got the characters in the shot. We have several technical aspects of the shots here. Things like the lens, the movement of the camera, the angle of the camera, the framing, depth of field. Dramatic context, the pacing we have, these AI agents are coming up with the image prompts in order to generate the anchor image as well as the video prompt to generate the video, resulting. Here's an example of a shot. We can see which characters in the scene, in this case, Paul, we can see the dialogue. We can play the dialogue, but we can also play the shot itself. This is my favorite part. Now, once we've produced all these shots, we can then talk to the AI agent. And have a collaborative conversation much in the same way that an engineer would have a conversation with a cursor or cloud code about their code base on how to make the next feature. In this case, I might ask something like Tell me about scene 3. And just like that, we have a detailed analysis that the agent was able to perform. Giving us a quick intro to scene 3, I can also ask a question like how can we add a shot or two to make this more Hitchcock in style? And we can see here. It's provided us with the basics of what a Hitchcock style is, and it's giving us some suggestions of some shots that we can do Now in order to create those shots, we can either go in here and manually create the shot ourselves, or we can ask the agent to compose the shots for us. And so the idea is that as a filmmaker, you've got about 80% of the shots composed for you. And through a conversation with these AI agents, you can dial in the shots to the style that really tells the story the way you envision it. Now, this is just a prototype at this point, but this gives us an idea of how we can use advanced AI reasoning agents to build shot lists and save weeks of manual labor in this process and make it ultimately faster and. More intuitive and more fun for novices and professional film makers alike.

comments.text: Sharing every prompt and the skill file is a generous move, and it turns this film into a study guide for anyone learning AI filmmaking. Keeping polar night dark is the craft problem I'd point students to first. Video models drift toward even, bright exposure, so building the pipeline around firelight and starlight as the only sources is real cinematography thinking. Blocking the camera in Blender before each Seedance shot also gives the edit a shot plan it can rely on, which most AI shorts are missing. I'm curious how the language dictionary in the Claude skill held up across 20 minutes of generated dialogue. Did Seedance keep the pronunciation of words from the film's language consistent from scene to scene, or did you have to regenerate lines to fix drift? One commenter also asked about the total cost in time and tokens. A rough count of generations per finished minute would be one of the most useful numbers anyone could publish right now, since it's what people planning their first long-form piece need most.

posts.description:
This 20-min drama is the most realistic AI movie we've EVER made 🔥

ANERNEQ is an Arctic drama about love, sacrifice and the cost of letting go. A young huntress leads her father, whose fading mind mistakes her for his dead wife, across 1920s Chukotka to the sacred Whale Bone Alley.

Every frame is generated on Higgsfield AI, without cameras and actors.

The film takes place in polar night, and the only light comes from fire, stars and snow. Video models default to flooding a scene with even, bright light, so most of the pipeline exists to keep it dark. All dialogue is generated too.

Blender set the camera angles before each shot. Claude wrote every prompt with our skill, which holds the script, props, character voices and a dictionary for the films language. Seedance generated every shot and every line of dialogue.

I shared the full project in the comments, including every prompt and the skill we used. Feel free to use anything from it in your own work.

posts.description:
We just showcased the trailer of our first 95-minute feature film made entirely on Higgsfield in Cannes.

Hell Grind is a 95-minute sci-fi heist directed by Aitore Zholdaskali and co-written with Adilkhan Yerzhanov, a two-time Cannes Official Programme filmmaker. A team of 15 professional directors, DPs, and editors made it on Higgsfield in 14 days for under $500K. The traditional comparable production cost is around $50M.

But beyond the numbers, this is the first AI film to demonstrate that AI can now sustain character consistency, world coherence, and narrative arc across a complete feature.

Hell Grind screens at Cinema Olympia in Cannes on May 21!

posts.transcript: Obviously, I'm working for an AI studio now. We have multiple movies with multiple movies in production now, and the goal is to create a full feature. But you want to put in art in the front, you want human creativity up front, you want the actors to drive the performance. Don't want the jokes to be written by a machine. AI is a very, very strong tool to visualize things and to make things. But it will it guesses the picture and it will average if you if we'll find the average if you don't like, push it to do something unique. And you can only find something unique if you actually have artists. And we are, yeah, we've, we've recently, we have a film called The Most serious fart right now. That is an animated movie that the legacy studios didn't want to produce. Directed and written by Mike Bender. And yeah, we, we have 2D animate animators working on that right now making, making animations for the fart clouds. There is no way I model that, you know, it was trained on a fart cloud. posts.description:
“AI will never make movies like Disney.”

Well, we’re getting pretty close.

This animation was created by @EHuanglu using Seedance 2.5, and it’s impressive how far AI-generated animation has come.

Disney and Pixar spent decades mastering the art of animation, combining beautiful visuals with storytelling, creativity, and characters that people genuinely connect with.

And I think those things will matter just as much in the age of AI.

We’ll probably see an overwhelming amount of low-quality AI-generated movies and animations, just like the AI slop flooding social media today.

But for people who actually understand storytelling, have good taste, and know how to bring creative ideas to life, these tools are making the production process dramatically faster, cheaper, and more accessible.

AI is another tool in the evolution of animation. Disney was already reusing animation sequences back in the 1960s and 1970s to save time and money, and the industry later moved from hand-drawn animation to digital production.

Experienced animators and filmmakers already understand the principles that make great animation work, so they’ll likely have a head start in using AI creatively.

The technology will keep improving, but having access to the same tools doesn’t mean everyone will create equally good movies.

I’m excited to see what talented storytellers will create when the technical and financial barriers become smaller.

Follow me AI Agentixz for more.

comments.text:
Movies, like music, work because we empathise with the characters and the story telling, so while we can debate doing a posh story board using these tools I think, as is the case with all true human artists, the final cut - acted, filmed, directed and edited would bring a dimension of nuance AI wont get. It’s been the same for ever increasing computer game graphics. The people still aren’t right. We can tell. 

But I say let the market decide. If an AI movie moves you and you then find out it’s AI I’m not sure how I’d approach that, but it’s not happened yet. As for slop - sure - have you seen the slop Disney has been churning out for years? It’s a conveyer belt of derivative mediocrity. And that’s pre AI.

My point is AI will never make a great movie because that requires humans to act in them. We’re a long way off AI faking that. 

Just my 2c. 

AI is here and even as I agree with the sentiment, getting on our soap boxes about it won’t help because there’s plenty of people will pay for the slop I guess.
comments.author: Roger Foxcroft

posts.description:
I made this short film with Claude Opus 5.5 and Higgsfield AI MCP in about 90 minutes.

5.5 is really very good at AI movie generation, and it's become a much easier thing to get into in the last few months.

Process:

1. Give Claude Opus 5.5 an overall brief - loose shot plan and script idea.
2. It'll create a scene plan which can be converted into a skill.
3. Ask it to produce a storyboard in GPT Image 2.5.
4. Much back and forth here finessing shots (time consuming bit).
5. When happy, ask it to generate the video and stitch together.
6. Claude can do sound FX and music. 🤯
7. Review the video, ask it to change scenes (a bit like step 4).

It cost $10 to make this 1 minute sequence in Higgsfield credits.

It's not perfect yet - I need to rerun step 7 particularly on the robot charge part, but it's not exactly terrible. I'm going to make a 10 minute short.

I find it frighteningly good and its job, hence the topic of the video.

Where will we end up by 2030?
